title: 中国外来植物的物种组成、区系特征及影响因素分析
author: 张金梦, 朱亮亮, 印浩楠, 王丽, 刘玉莉.中国外来植物的物种组成、区系特征及影响因素分析.广西植物:https://chinaxiv.org/abs/202503.00204.[ChinaXiv:202503.00204V1]
description: 中国外来植物的物种组成、区系特征及影响因素分析 后印本 Species composition, floristic characteristics and influencing factors of alien plants in China 作者： 张金梦 1 朱亮亮 1 印浩楠 1 王丽 1 刘玉莉 2* 作者单位： 1. 江苏第二师范学院地理科学学院，南京211200 2. 湖州师范学院可持续发展研究院，浙江湖州313000 提交时间： 2025-03-19 11:24:41 摘要: 中国是遭受生物入侵危害和威胁最严重的国家之一，掌握全国尺度上外来植物的物 种组成、区系特征及其影响因素对减少外来植物的入侵风险和促进防控管理至关重要。该文 以《中国外来植物数据集》为基础，统计分析其物种组成、生活型、区系类型等特征，并利 用相关性分析和逐步回归模型深入探究了社会经济和生态因素与外来植物之间的关联机理。 结果表明：（1）我国已有的外来植物中大型科（99 科，13 741 种）和大型属（205 属，7 199 种）对总物种数的贡献率分别为93.41%和48.94%。从生活型组成看，草本植物构成了我国 外来植物的主体，占比59.82%。（2）全国范围内热带成分科占据明显优势，占总科数的 52.65%；其次分别为温带成分科（21.56%）和世界广布科（20.49%）。（3）外来植物总数 的分布格局支持了各区系成分科的分布格局，即东部沿海和西南地区的外来植物总数和各区 系成分最丰富，向内陆减少。然而，北方省市的世界广布和温带成分科的比重较高，南方省 市的热带成分科的占比最高。（4）相关性分析表明入侵植物所在科的入侵种数与该科所包 含的外来种数存在显著正相关关系。各省市经济因素和气候条件共同决定了我国外来植物总 数和各区系成分科数的空间分布格局，但各区系成分占比主要受热量条件（年均温）的影响。 未来我国应大力加强对具有热带性质和世界广布的大科、大属的草本植物的引种评估与监管。 外来植物 区系成分 物种组成 多样性 分布格局 分类： 生物学 >> 植物学 >> 应用植物学 期刊： 广西植物 投稿状态： 已在期刊出版 引用： ChinaXiv:202503.00204 (或此版本 ChinaXiv:202503.00204V1 ) DOI:10.11931/guihaia.gxzw202405030 CSTR:32003.36.ChinaXiv.202503.00204 推荐引用方式： 张金梦,朱亮亮,印浩楠,王丽,刘玉莉.中国外来植物的物种组成、区系特征及影响因素分析.广西植物:https://chinaxiv.org/abs/202503.00204.[ChinaXiv:202503.00204V1] 版本历史 [V1] 2025-03-19 11:24:41 ChinaXiv:202503.00204V1 下载全文

description: This paper delineats the portrayal of Sita in Amish Tripathy's novel ' Sita: The Warrior of Mithila' and her relevance in the' Ramayana' where Sita is depicted as a devoted wife,daughter and a silent visionary. She is always behind the customs and traditions which may be relevant in that particular  context. She is full of love and compassion and her patience can be judged with the fact that she accepts meekly what is imposed on her . She remains  as pure as Gangajal in spite of so many hardships and ordeal in her life. Religion is every thing to him. Tripathy's Sita is endowed with extraordinary courage ,wisdom,devotion,love,compassion,martial art, war strategy and physical strength. She is ready to break all the 'Man Centred shackles'. She is able to rule , enjoy her strength and independence. Amish has his own vision and thinking which brings her out in the ' Forest of Enchantments' where she presents her in bold terms . Coming out in new horizon has different connotations-Sita not only puts her feet boldly in an alien world but she remains virtouos and optimistic in different unforeseen circumstances. She is a torch bearer for the whole class by representing her strong values, patience,devotion,mititary art and novel thinking.

title: ERIC ED581044: Proceedings of the 2015 Annual Meeting of the Canadian Mathematics Education Study Group = Actes De La Rencontre Annuelle 2015 Du Groupe Canadien D'etude en Didactique Des Mathematiques (39th, Moncton, New Brunswick, Canada, June 5-9, 2015)
author: ERIC
description: This submission contains the Proceedings of the 2015 Annual Meeting of the Canadian Mathematics Education Study Group (CMESG), held at the Université de Moncton in Moncton, New Brunswick. The CMESG is a group of mathematicians and mathematics educators who meet annually to discuss mathematics education issues at all levels of learning. The aims of the Study Group are: to advance education by organizing and coordinating national conferences and seminars to study and improve the theories of the study of mathematics or any other aspects of mathematics education in Canada at all levels; and to undertake research in mathematics education and to disseminate the results of this research. These proceedings include plenary lectures, an elder talk memoire, panel discussions, working group reports, topic sessions, new PhD reports, and summaries of ad hoc and poster sessions. Papers include: (1) Diversité, variabilité et convergence des pratiques enseignantes/Diversity, Variability, and Commonalities Among Teaching Practices (Éric Roditi) [Written in French]; (2) Connections: Mathematical, Interdisciplinary, Electronic, and Personal (Deborah Hughes Hallet); (3) Task Design and Problem Posing (Ami Mamolo and John McLoughlin); (4) Indigenous Ways of Knowing in Mathematics (Lisa Lunney Borden and Florence Glanfield); (5) Theoretical Frameworks in Mathematics Education Research/Les cadres théoriques dans la recherche en didactique des mathématiques (Jérôme Proulx and Anna Sierpinska) [Written in English and French]; (6) Early Years Teaching, Learning and Research: Tensions in Adult-Child Interactions Around Mathematics (Ann Anderson and Helena P. Osana); (7) Innovations in Tertiary Mathematics Teaching, Learning and Research/Innovations au post-secondaire pour l'enseignement, l'apprentissage et la recherché (Taras Gula and Denis Tanguay) [Written in English and French]; (8) Some Thoughts on Mathematics as the Alien Word (Richard Barwell); (9) Interaction Between a Mathematics Department in a University and the School System/Interaction entre un département de mathématiques universitaire et le système scolaire (Paul Deguire) [Written in English and French]; (10) Building Thinking Classrooms: Conditions for Problem Solving (Peter Liljedahl); (11) Growing Mathematical Understanding and Folding Back: The Individual, the Collective, the Teacher (Lyndon Martin); (12) De la « clochette de vigilance » au changement de posture: Quelques questions issues de la didactique des mathématiques et étudiées depuis la didactique du sens commun/From the Use of an "Alert Bell" to a Change of Posture: Some Questions Emerging from the Didactics of Mathematics Being Studied by the Didactics of Common Sense (Sophie René de Cotret) [Written in French and English]; (13) Secondary School Mathematics Teacher Candidates' Research, Pedagogical, and Content Knowledge (Alexander Antropov); (14) Étude des significations de la multiplication pour différents ensembles de nombres dans un contexte de géométrisation…et un aperçu de quelques réflexions d'ordre épistémologique (Raquel Isabel Barrera Curin) [Written in French]; (15) The Role of Drawing in Arithmetic Word Problem Solving: Microanalysis of the Subject/Material Dialectic (Élysée-Robert Cadet); (16) Histoire des mathématiques dans la formation des enseignants du secondaire : Une narration polyphonique sur la fragilité, l'adversité et l'empathie--Résumé de thèse/History of Mathematics in a Preservice Teacher's Training Context: A Polyphonic Narration on Fragility, Adversity and Empathy--Thesis Summary (David Guillemette) [Written in French and English]; (17) Improving Mathematics Teaching Through Professional Learning Groups (Jennifer Holm); (18) Mathematics Problems and Thinking Mathematically in Undergraduate Education (Asia R. Matthews); (19) Understanding Learning in Mathematics Through the Metaphor of Authoring (P. Janelle McFeetors); (20) How Elementary Students Learn to Mathematically Analyze Word Problems: The Case of Addition and Subtraction (Elena Polotskaia); (21) Le concept de variabilité chez des enseignants de mathématiques au secondaire (Sylvain Vermette) [Written in French]; (22) Lesson and Learning Study: Collaborative Learning Structures for Preservice Teacher Education (Diana Royea); and (23) Hear My Voice: Teachers' Stories (Ann Kajander and Jennifer Holm). Individual papers contain references. [For the 2014 proceedings, see ED581042.]

O Espírito Santo, de forma geral, é o estado que lidera a produção e exportação de rochas ornamentais no país.  *🔍 FIQUE SABENDO* 🗣 "Tenro" é um adjetivo que descreve algo que é macio, mole, suave ao toque ou fácil de cortar, geralmente usado para alimentos, especialmente carnes, frutas ou vegetais. Quando dizemos que uma carne está tenra, significa que ela está bem cozida, macia e fácil de mastigar. Também pode ser usado de forma figurada para se referir a algo delicado, sensível ou em estágio inicial de desenvolvimento, como em "idade tenra" (idade jovem ou infância) ou "tenro sentimento" (emoção ainda nova ou sensível) FONTE: IA *✈️ TURISMO* 🏙 Cuiabá, capital do estado de Mato Grosso, é um destino que surpreende pela diversidade cultural, história rica e localização estratégica. Conhecida como “Portal da Amazônia”, a cidade é também um importante ponto de acesso ao Pantanal, à Chapada dos Guimarães e à Floresta Amazônica, tornando-se um excelente ponto de partida para o ecoturismo no Brasil. Fundada no século XVIII durante o ciclo do ouro, Cuiabá ainda preserva traços da arquitetura colonial em seu centro histórico, com igrejas, casarões e praças que contam a história da ocupação da região. O clima é quente e seco durante boa parte do ano, o que impulsiona atividades ao ar livre, como passeios pelos parques urbanos, como o Parque Mãe Bonifácia e o Parque Tia Nair, que oferecem trilhas, áreas de lazer e contato com a natureza no meio da cidade. [02/07/2025 06:03] Marcos Vinicius: Além das belezas naturais, a cultura cuiabana é marcada pela forte influência indígena, africana e portuguesa. Isso se reflete na gastronomia típica, com pratos como a farofa de banana, o mojica de pintado, o arroz com pequi e o tradicional peixe assado, todos preparados com ingredientes locais. A cidade também é famosa por suas festas populares e danças tradicionais, como o siriri e o cururu. Para quem busca aventura e natureza, Cuiabá está a cerca de 70 km da Chapada dos Guimarães, um dos mais belos parques nacionais do Brasil, conhecido por suas formações rochosas, cachoeiras e mirantes espetaculares. Ao sul, o Pantanal oferece experiências únicas com safáris fotográficos, observação de aves e passeios de barco por entre a vida selvagem. Com sua localização privilegiada, calor humano e riqueza cultural, Cuiabá é um destino que conquista tanto os amantes da natureza quanto os interessados em história e tradição brasileira.  FONTE: IA *🍽 CULINARIA* *🍽 Nome do prato: Tutu de Feijão* 🥛 Ingredientes: 2 xícaras de feijão cozido (com caldo) 1 xícara de farinha de mandioca (ou de milho, se preferir) 1 cebola média picada 2 dentes de alho picados 100g de bacon picado 1 linguiça calabresa fatiada 2 colheres de sopa de óleo ou banha Sal e pimenta-do-reino a gosto Cheiro-verde picado para finalizar 🥄 Modo de preparo: Em uma panela, aqueça o óleo (ou a banha) e doure o bacon. Acrescente a linguiça calabresa e frite até ficar bem dourada. Em seguida, junte a cebola e o alho, refogando até ficarem macios. Adicione o feijão cozido com um pouco do caldo (se estiver muito grosso, adicione um pouco de água). Misture bem e deixe ferver por alguns minutos. Aos poucos, acrescente a farinha, mexendo sempre para não empelotar, até atingir uma consistência cremosa, nem muito líquida, nem muito seca. Ajuste o sal e a pimenta. Finalize com cheiro-verde picado e sirva quente, como acompanhamento de carnes, arroz ou couve refogada.  FONTE: IA

title: ERIC EJ1057352: A Defining Moment in E-Working: The Application of an E-Working Definition to the Education Context
author: ERIC
description: Using qualitative data gathered through 144 questionnaires completed online by education sector personnel, this paper examines the relevance of a definition of e-working to the educational context. It identifies that the definition, which draws on and extends existing knowledge and identifies e-working to be a way of being a worker as well as a way or a mechanism for carrying out the work task, has clear potential to be applied within the education sector. The paper identifies that it is not the composite elements of the definition which may appear alien to the worker in the educational context, but instead inference drawn from the way in which the e-working term has hitherto been regarded.

title: Goodbye East End : an evacuee's story
author: Merron, David, author
description: 364 pages ; 20 cm, "As Hitler's bombs rained down hell during World War 2, eight-year-old David Merron was taken from the heart of his close-knit Jewish community in London's East End and evacuated to the safety of the English countryside. Transplanted into an alien world, adrift from his nurturing family and at the mercy of sometimes cold-hearted strangers, life was frightening and lonely. The strangeness of this new existence - its religious and cultural shifts - left David confused and questioning not only his faith but his very sense of self. But, with time, David realised that the rural world was also beautiful. Far from the cramped and often poverty-stricken East End, the countryside was wild and wonderful - an adventure playground in which a curious lad was free to flourish. Immersed in the ebb and flow of country life, David harboured a secret. Increasingly, he didn't want to return to the dirty streets of the East End. Sometimes, he didn't want the war to end. David's moving memoir is about a small boy's burgeoning love of the countryside and the confusion he felt about not missing - and not missing - home. Set against a wartime backdrop of flaming skies and pluming black smoke, it is a celebration of the wonder and tranquility of the natural world that changed the shape of his life."--Publisher's description

title: XIO3 Garden City Atari Computer Enthusiasts Newsletter January / February 1995
description: In this issue: Atari News and Rumours by Rowland Grant: In 1994, Atari lowered its expectations for the Jaguar game system from 1,000,000 Jaguars sold with 50 games to 200, 000 Jaguars sold with 20 games . / For the third quarter of 1994, Atari reported net sales of $7.1 million, incurring a net loss of $3.9 million. Sam Tramiel said, “ T he loss in the recent quarter was a result of delays in software releases as well as expenses related to promotional activity.” He further said, “ I t’s absolutely not a problem now, and y ou will see lots and lots of software titles coming out soon.” / Atari has received regulatory approval for its litigation agreement with Sega, and the financial transaction is now closed, with Atari gaining about $90 million. / M.D. Sass Investors predicts Atari shares will drop to less than three dollars early in 1995 and that Atari will be forced to write down its Jaguar game system. / At the end of 1994, Atari’s shares were hovering around $4. / Matsushita has dropped the price on their R*E*A*L 3DO console from $700 to $400. Despite extensive advertising, Matsushita has n ot yet achieved profitability in the US market. 3DO ha s achiev ed success in the Japan ese market, but Sony and Sega have now introduced their new game systems . / Time Warner Cable’s Full Service Network (FSN) has agreed to provide Jaguar video games on its interactive cable system. / Virtuality Group PLC, a British designer of virtual reality systems, has agreed to produce a prototype virtual reality headset for Atari. It may be available by Christmas 1995 for $200. / Toys R Us stores will carry the Jaguar. Atari has placed Jaguar demonstration kiosks in all 25 Toys R Us stores in Japan. / There are rumours that the Atari warehouse in Holland has been closed. / Early in November, the Alien vs Predator game for the Jaguar became available. Sam Tramiel has stated, “ I n less than three weeks, over 50 percent of our installed base has purchased A V P.” One reviewer rated Club Drive as “so bad it’s good.” Jaguar Doom is considered outstanding. Iron Soldier made an appearance in December, and it is a winner. Kasumi Ninja has been criticized for its control response. There are rumours that more games would have been available in December, but the ROM chip maker couldn’t handle the last-minute rush. / A Defender coin- operated machine has been installed in Jeff Minter’s apartment to help him with programming Defender 2000 for the Jaguar . / BioVision technology was used for the creation of the martial arts moves for the Fight for Life game. / Trip Hawkins, President of 3DO, says, “to be a real competitor in the game market, you need $500 million in capital.” / Atari is still shipping Falcon computers, and at the usual list price. / C-Labs intends to manufacture music workstations in Germany. / Wizztronics has sold more than 300 rack-mount cases for the ST/Falcons. / Wizztronics has released a device called Hotfoot, allowing MIDI users to have remote pedal control of the ST or Falcon keyboard. / Atari produced a prototype CD-ROM unit, but a lack of interest from ST users caused Atari to terminate the project. / In the present time, Toad Computers advertises CD drives with an included interface and software for ST/TT/Falcon computers. / Universal Item Selector Version IV can handle files on a CD. / MagiC is discussed. / There are rumours that Gadgets by Small has gone bankrupt due to a lost lawsuit. / The last edition of ST Review will be the January 1995 issue. / ST Format and ST Applications continue to be published. P EEK ing Around (Gossip Column) by Gordon F. Hooper: The club received a newsletter from the Winnipeg ST Users Group. It had an ad for Computer Direct, a firm located in Spruce Grove, Alberta. It calls itself “Canada’s Atari computer source.” The price is $5 for their catalogue. Library Report by Ted Skrecky: Craig Carmichael has produced a demo version of his multitasking OME n operating system, which will be added to the GCACE ST software catalogue. Allan Shura was at the last club meeting, and he distributed a demo copy of his new strategy wargame, The Power and the Gory. ( U pdate: I checked the original N eotrek Software Ltd. demo disk d ated 17/11/94, and it can no longer be read. A no-name bulk disk was used, and t hose disks are usually the first to go “bad.” However, the demo was added to GCACE disk #159. The Atari Mania website has the August 1996 ST Format review for this game.) / In Victoria, MicroPlay sold six Jaguar systems, including their demo model. They have an entire case filled with Jaguar games. Both Alien vs Predator and Doom are helping to sell Jaguar s . Third-party hardware, such as the Catbox and Jagdapter are on order. / Doom and Iron Soldier will be demoed at the next GCACE meeting. GCACE Meetings by Rowland Grant: Alien vs Predator was demoed at George Rose’s Social SIG. Rowland’s comments regarding this game should be of interest to Jaguar AVP game enthusiasts . / Alien vs Predator and Wolfenstein 3D were demoed at the November meeting. Allan Shura of Neotrek Software Ltd. distributed demo copies of his game, The Power and the Gory. He wrote it using GFA Basic and assembler. The game’s box art was also shown. / Craig Carmichael of Esquimalt Digital Logic Inc. has released OMEn 3.03. The full version of OMEn for the ST/TT/Falcon is $44.00 CDN (plus PST and GST). C omputer Languages by Douglas Skrecky: The ideal computer language would understand what you wish to create and automatically translate those wishes into reality. Perhaps one day we will see computers that can program themselves. Numerous computer languages are discussed, such as Cobol, C, Objective C, C++, ADA (supported by the D epartment of D efence and has been upgraded to ADA9X.), PL1, Algol (both PL1 and Algol have gone extinct), Smalltalk (sponsored by Xerox but, despite high programmer productivity, has not been a success ), Modula- 2, Modula-3, Oberon-3, Parasol, Sather, Eiffel, and Microsoft BASIC. Atari 8-Bit Affairs by Rowland Grant: The MIO II board attaches to the parallel bus of an 800XL, allowing for the use of an IDE hard drive. / The Sweet 16 board contains a 65816 microprocessor, which is a plug-in replacement for the 6502C in the Atari XL/XE computers. / New Atari User magazine is now considerably reduced in size, and large program listings will not be printed. / Tom Hunt has released several file storage utilities. / The Quick compiler is popular in Germany, especially since Action! carts are hard to get and are very expensive. / The Atari Classic Programmers Club (ACPC) has released the Atari Developer’s Operating System (ADOS), which provides for a windowing environment. / Jim Drew is developing an Atari 8-bit emulator for the Commodore Amiga. BONUS: This issue of XIO3 mentioned Alan Shura’s The Power and the Gory wargame for Atari ST computers. At the November 1994 GCACE meeting, Alan distributed the demo version on disk. PGDEMO.LZH has been included in this XIO3 newsletter archive along with UNLZH172.PRG. Click on SHOW ALL under the DOWNLOAD OPTIONS section to access these two files. Transfer both files to an Atari ST computer. Do not put the game files in a folder. Decompress the LZH file to the root directory of a disk. Newsletter scanned and uploaded by Ted Skrecky (Victoria, BC, CANADA). Note: Many Atari-related newsletters, etc, have been uploaded to Internet Archive. To discover what I have uploaded, do a search for "Ted Skrecky."

author: Alistair Shearer
description: To the Hindu, the entire universe is a living being, and through the visual arts - ritualistic, compelling, often stunningly beautiful - that holistic awareness is made available to all. Long rejected by the West as alien and bizarre, Hindu imagery speaks a language that is at last beginning to be understood. Its extraordinary symbolism - elephant-headed and multi-armed deities, fierce demons and fabulous creatures - is a sophisticated iconography conveying universal religious truths. Uniting sensuousness and spirituality, passion and detachment, Hinduism celebrates the fullness of life, and teaches the indivisibility of body and soul, time and eternity. title: ERIC ED040810: Texas Migrant Labor. Annual Report, 1969.
author: ERIC
description: Among the responsibilities of the Good Neighbor Commission of Texas are (1) a survey of conditions and (2) a study of problems related to migrant labor in Texas. This annual report of the 1969 migrant scene shows the results of that survey and study. Beginning with an overview of Texas migrant labor, which goes back several years and includes a current map of travel patterns, the report takes up Texas agricultural and migrant labor. Migrant programs are cited with descriptions of their goals and funding agencies. The Migrant Farm Labor Center in Hope, Arkansas, is described as an example of a full-service center, for the benefit of the migrant farm worker and his family. Information on alien labor and immigration is presented next and touches on legal and illegal commuting. Current developments are discussed in terms of migrant child education, adult migrant education, migrant teacher preparation, bilingual education, housing, health, border industrialization in Mexico, and migrant economics. Trends in migration and a summary of data complete the report. (BD)

description: THE $1.28 TRILLION CREDIT CARD DEBT EXTRACTION MACHINE The United States credit card system is not a free market. It is an engineered extraction machine that transfers 496‑496‑789 million per day from struggling families to banks and wealthy cardholders. Every component is legal. Every component is intentional. And the result is a reverse‑Robin‑Hood wealth transfer that has persisted for 40 years. THE DOUBLE TAXATION TRAP Section 163(h) of the Internal Revenue Code prohibits individual taxpayers from deducting credit card interest. A family earning $50,000 pays interest with after‑tax dollars – the IRS takes its cut first via payroll withholding, then the bank takes its 21‑24% APR. The same family is taxed twice on the same money: once when earned, once when borrowed to survive. Banks, however, deduct defaulted debt from taxable income under Sections 166 and 585, reducing their liability by 21% of every dollar charged off. The IRS Large Business & International Division issued Directive 04‑1014‑008 instructing auditors “generally should not challenge” bank bad‑debt deductions – categorical non‑enforcement that has never been applied to any other industry. THE ARITHMETIC OF EXTRACTION Total credit card debt peaked at $1.28 trillion in Q4 2025 (Federal Reserve Bank of New York). Average APRs stand at 21.5%. $181‑$250 billion in interest paid in 2025 alone. Credit card return on assets (ROA) averages 6.8%. $30 billion annual regressive transfer from cash/debit users to credit card users, with $9.2 billion flowing directly from households earning under $150,000 to those earning over $150,000. Minimum payments are designed at 1‑2% of balance, ensuring decades of debt for those who can least afford it. YOUR INTEREST PAYS FOR FIRST CLASS FLIGHTS AND AIRPORT LOUNGES That $30 billion transfer is not an abstraction. It pays for the free flights, upgraded hotel rooms, and luxury airport lounge access enjoyed by wealthy cardholders who pay their balances in full every month. The Chase Sapphire Reserve, Citi Premier, Capital One Venture, and American Express Platinum – their most lucrative perks are funded directly by the interest extracted from families who cannot afford to pay off their cards. Every time a struggling family makes a minimum payment, a fraction of that money flows upstream to subsidize a rich person’s vacation. The poor pay. The rich fly free. That is the engine. Minimum payments are designed at 1‑2% of balance, ensuring decades of debt for those who can least afford it. THE TAX SHIELD ASSEMBLY Banks employ four overlapping mechanisms to pay near‑zero tax on this interest revenue. First, the bad‑debt deduction (§166) reduces taxable income by the full amount of charged‑off balances – $57.6 billion in 2025 alone, saving banks $12.1 billion. Second, the IRS safe harbor guarantees no audit of these deductions. Third, the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 allows banks to purchase transferable green energy tax credits from developers, offsetting remaining liability. SolarEdge, founded by Unit 8200 veterans Guy Sella and Lior Handelsman, is a primary beneficiary. Fourth, banks shift profits through subsidiaries in Ireland, Cayman Islands, and Bermuda – tax havens that account for over 20% of cross‑border banking debt. title: ERIC ED455992: The Legal Construction of Race: Mexican-Americans and Whiteness. Occasional Paper No. 54. Latino Studies Series.
author: ERIC
description: Mexican Americans were legally defined as Whites as a result of treaty obligations with Mexico that expressly allowed Mexicans to become U.S. citizens. Federal laws of the time required that an alien be White to become a U.S. citizen. The government of Mexico and the U.S. Department of State pressured the U.S. Census Bureau to reclassify Mexican Americans as White. In a Texas school desegregation case, the court held that Mexican American children could not be segregated on a racial basis but did permit segregation on the basis of linguistic difficulties or migrant status. Historically, institutions controlled by dominant groups have determined the legal definitions of racial groups and imposed those definitions in ways that maintained the status quo. The law recognizes racial group identity when such identity is a basis for exclusion and subordination but often refuses to recognize group identity when asserted as a basis for affirming rights and resisting subordination. Examples of this can be seen in a Texas court ruling that imposed a definition of "White" on Mexican Americans protesting their exclusion from grand and petit juries as a distinct group, and in a court rejection of Mexican American claims for class representation in a class action suit seeking equal educational opportunities. Although Mexican Americans have been legally constructed as White, this legal status has had only marginal impact on daily life because of colonial discourses constructing Mexican Americans as racially "other." (Contains 99 endnotes.) (TD)

title: The Neuro-Ecology of Drosophila Pupation Behavior.
author: Del Pino, Francisco, Jara, Claudia, Pino, Luis, Godoy-Herrera, Raul
description: This article is from PLoS ONE , volume 9 . Abstract Many species of Drosophila form conspecific pupa aggregations across the breeding sites. These aggregations could result from species-specific larval odor recognition. To test this hypothesis we used larval odors of D. melanogaster and D. pavani, two species that coexist in the nature. When stimulated by those odors, wild type and vestigial (vg) third-instar larvae of D. melanogaster pupated on conspecific larval odors, but individuals deficient in the expression of the odor co-receptor Orco randomly pupated across the substrate, indicating that in this species, olfaction plays a role in pupation site selection. Larvae are unable to learn but can smell, the Syn97CS and rut strains of D. melanogaster, did not respond to conspecific odors or D. pavani larval cues, and they randomly pupated across the substrate, suggesting that larval odor-based learning could influence the pupation site selection. Thus, Orco, Syn97CS and rut loci participated in the pupation site selection. When stimulated by conspecific and D. melanogaster larval cues, D. pavani larvae also pupated on conspecific odors. The larvae of D. gaucha, a sibling species of D. pavani, did not respond to D. melanogaster larval cues, pupating randomly across the substrate. In nature, D. gaucha is isolated from D. melanogaster. Interspecific hybrids, which result from crossing pavani female with gaucha males clumped their pupae similarly to D. pavani, but the behavior of gaucha female x pavani male hybrids was similar to D. gaucha parent. The two sibling species show substantial evolutionary divergence in organization and functioning of larval nervous system. D. melanogaster and D. pavani larvae extracted information about odor identities and the spatial location of congener and alien larvae to select pupation sites. We hypothesize that larval recognition contributes to the cohabitation of species with similar ecologies, thus aiding the organization and persistence of Drosophila species guilds in the wild.

title: Effect of the Internet Commerce on Dispersal Modes of Invasive Alien Species.
author: Lenda, Magdalena, Skorka, Piotr, Knops, Johannes M. H., Moron, Dawid, Sutherland, William J., Kuszewska, Karolina, Woyciechowski, Michal
description: This article is from PLoS ONE , volume 9 . Abstract The spread of invasive alien plants has considerable environmental and economic consequences, and is one of the most challenging ecological problems. The spread of invasive alien plant species depends largely on long-distance dispersal, which is typically linked with human activity. The increasing domination of the internet will have impacts upon almost all components of our lives, including potential consequences for the spread of invasive species. To determine whether the rise of Internet commerce has any consequences for the spread of invasive alien plant species, we studied the sale of thirteen of some of the most harmful Europe invasive alien plant species sold as decorative plants from twenty-eight large, well known gardening shops in Poland that sold both via the Internet and through traditional customer sales. We also analyzed temporal changes in the number of invasive plants sold in the largest Polish internet auction portal. When sold through the Internet invasive alien plant species were transported considerably longer distances than for traditional sales. For internet sales, seeds of invasive alien plant species were transported further than were live plants saplings; this was not the case for traditional sales. Also, with e-commerce the shape of distance distribution were flattened with low skewness comparing with traditional sale where the distributions were peaked and right-skewed. Thus, e-commerce created novel modes of long-distance dispersal, while traditional sale resembled more natural dispersal modes. Moreover, analysis of sale in the biggest Polish internet auction portal showed that the number of alien specimens sold via the internet has increased markedly over recent years. Therefore internet commerce is likely to increase the rate at which ecological communities become homogenized and increase spread of invasive species by increasing the rate of long distance dispersal.

title: ERIC EJ846484: Canadian Postcolonialism: Recovering British Roots
author: ERIC
description: The field of Postcolonial Studies is one of the academic fashions that has arisen in an attempt to amend or replace radical theories of social power since the alleged discrediting of Marxism. The Canadian case is more ambiguous. Postcolonialism, already an essentially contested concept, is especially conflicted where Canada is concerned. Canada has certainly had a colonial past, with parts of its territory having been claimed by one European power or another since Giovanni Caboto (alias Jean Cabot, a.k.a. John Cabot) landed in Newfoundland in 1497. Canada, however, is unlike countries such as Peru, Congo, Iraq, India, and Malaysia whose indigenous populations were politically repressed and economically exploited during long periods of alien cultural domination. As Cynthia Sugars (2004) has pointed out, like other "settler-invaded cultures," the application of postcolonial methodology is problematic because of Canada's "location within the industrialized West [and] because of its treatment of its aboriginal peoples and other minorities. [So], questions proliferate: Is Canada postcolonial? Who in Canada is postcolonial? Are some Canadians more postcolonial than others?" Elements of this story have cropped up in the work of the widely respected US sociologist, Seymour Martin Lipset. The genuine and original "Canadian identity," Lipset says, is "the result of a victorious counterrevolution, and in a sense must justify its raison d'etre by emphasizing the virtues of being separate from the United States."

title: Serum TGF-?1 and SMAD3 levels are closely associated with coronary artery disease.
author: Chen, Can, Lei, Wei, Chen, Wenjiang, Zhong, Jianfeng, Gao, Xiaoxin, Li, Bo, Wang, Huailong, Huang, Congxin
description: This article is from BMC Cardiovascular Disorders , volume 14 . Abstract Background: Coronary artery disease (CAD) is one of the most common diseases leading to mortality and morbidity worldwide. There is considerable debate on whether serum transforming growth factor β1 (TGF-β1) levels are associated with long-term major adverse cardiovascular events in patients with CAD, and to date, no study has specifically addressed levels in patients with different degrees of CAD severity. Methods: Serum TGF-β1 and mothers against decapentaplegic homolog 3 (SMAD3) concentrations were evaluated in 279 patients with CAD and 268 controls without CAD. The clinical and biochemical characteristics of all subjects were also determined and analyzed. Results: TGF-β1 and SMAD3 concentrations in CAD patients were significantly higher than those in the controls. The serum TGF-β1 level in acute myocardial infarction (AMI) was significantly higher than that in both stable angina pectoris (SAP) and unstable angina pectoris (UAP) (p < 0.05), while there was no marked difference between levels in SAP and UAP (p > 0.05). SMAD3 levels showed no obvious difference among AMI, SAP, and UAP. TGF-β1 and SMAD3 are potential biomarkers for CAD, and may be more accurate than Lpa, ApoA1, uric acid, BUN, or triglycerides (TG). Conclusions: Serum TGF-β1 and SMAD3 levels are closely associated with CAD, and may become useful biomarkers for diagnosis and risk stratification.

title: Revenger

description: 425 pages ; 25 cm, The galaxy has seen great empires rise and fall. Planets have shattered and been remade. Amongst the ruins of alien civilisations, building our own from the rubble, humanity still thrives. And there are vast fortunes to be made, if you know where to find them ... Captain Rackamore and his crew do. It's their business to find the tiny, enigmatic worlds which have been hidden away, booby-trapped, surrounded with layers of protection - and to crack them open for the ancient relics and barely-remembered technologies inside. But while they ply their risky trade with integrity, not everyone is so scrupulous. Adrana and Fura Ness are the newest members of Rackamore's crew, signed on to save their family from bankruptcy. Only Rackamore has enemies, and there might be more waiting for them in space than adventure and fortune: the fabled and feared Bosa Sennen in particular. Revenger is a science fiction adventure story set in the rubble of our solar system in the dark, distant future - a tale of space pirates, buried treasure and phantom weapons, of unspeakable hazards and single-minded heroism ... and of vengeance ..

title: HM 01079, Missal, for Cistercian use
description: San Marino, Huntington Library, HM 01079. Text(s): Missal, for Cistercian use. Description: ff. i + 141 (with f. 108 bis) + i - Bound in dark red morocco by Zaehnsdorf. - Written for a Cistercian abbey in Bohemia, as indicated by the Alleluia verses of the Sundays after Pentecost and by the saints of the sanctorale; Margaret, placed at 13 July (on f. 84v, between the Seven Brothers and the Divisio Apostolorum) rather than at 20 July, also suggests an origin in the Germanic area of Europe. The date of the copying may lie between 1252 (when Adalbert of Prague was inscribed in the Cistercian calendar) and 1255 (when the feast of Stanislas was introduced in the Cistercian calendar; here it has been added in the lower margin of f. 65). The book may have belonged at a later time to a monastery of Benedictine nuns: on f. 55v is an added line, "Salvam fac ancillam tuam," with a tie mark to the office of Benedict. On the front pastedown, the bookplate of the Piedmontese Counts Cays di Giletta e Caselette, engraved by Teresa Ramis Ronzini of Turin (ca. 1810?). Belonged to Henry White; his sale, Sotheby's, 21 April 1902, lot 1510 to Quaritch; alien sequestrated property sale, Anderson, New York, 17 February 1919, n. 29 to G. D. Smith; precise source and date of acquisition by Henry E. Huntington unknown. - C. W. Dutschke with the assistance of R. H. Rouse et al., Guide to Medieval and Renaissance Manuscripts in the Huntington Library (San Marino, 1989). De Ricci, 89. Aspects of Medieval England, n. 38 open at f. 51. Part 1: ff. 1-141v (+ f. 108r-v bis). Description: - Parchment - 215 x 315 mm - First quire missing as shown by signatures, 2.

title: The red house
author: Haddon, Mark, 1962-
description: 359 pages (large print) ; 24 cm, The set up of Mark Haddon's brilliant new novel is simple: Richard, a wealthy doctor, invites his estranged sister Angela and her family to join his for a week at a vacation home in the English countryside. Richard has just re-married and inherited a wilful stepdaughter in the process; Angela has a feckless husband and three children who sometimes seem alien to her. All eight arrive with low expectations for a pleasant holiday. But because of Haddon's extraordinary narrative technique, the stories of these eight people are anything but simple. Told through the alternating viewpoints of each character, The Red House becomes a symphony of long-held grudges, fading dreams and rising hopes, tightly-guarded secrets and illicit desires, all adding up to a portrait of contemporary family life that is bittersweet, comic, and deeply felt, Standard print ed. originally published: London : Jonathan Cape, 2012

title: Reef Antlerworm
author: Alex Ries
description: Check out my Patreon for the development of this beasty! The first creature created with the help of my supporters there :) https://www.patreon.com/alexries “The Reef Antlerworm, a robust and ill-tempered marine predator with a broad distribution in the warmer waters of Chri-irah, has been of interest to birrin natural historians, and fishermen, for some time.  Reaching a maximum length of around 3 feet, this species, one of the larger of this group, is dwarfed by the more rarely encountered giants of the deeper oceans, still manages to dominate its shallow water habitat. Hunted by divers for thousands of years for both its meat and egg masses, scientific interest has been focused on its informative anatomically adaptations, which offer important clues into the early evolution of the quadrilaterians to which the birrin belong. Relying on surprise when hunting, the reef antlerworm insinuates itself among marine debris on reefs and wrecks, showing only the tips of its sensory tentacles and eyestalks as it waits for prey, predators or rivals. Any small creature that swims too close is rapidly subdued in an explosive tangle of tentacles that erupt from around the mouth. The huge ornamental jaws are opened during prey capture, both to threaten any opportunistic predators, and simply to make room for food to pass. Spines at the jaws’ base help push prey down the expansive gullet, most of which is swallowed whole.  The jaws, actually a slight encumbrance when feeding, come into their own when antlerworms meet one another. Prime hunting spots on a reef can be hard to come by, and prey concentrations can change with tides and seasons. There is a constant battle to secure the best reef hollows and caves, and the worms often leave their haunts to attempt to find somewhere more productive. If they find a more desirable site is already taken, both will rise up from the sea floor, jaws held wide, and face off. If one set of jaws is obviously larger than the other, the smaller worm will usually retreat. Evenly matched opponents, however begin by locking jaws and pushing one another to determine strength. If that is not enough, a furious and usually brief fight begins, each trying to injure the other. The loser, sometimes fatally wounded, retreats. If no longer mobile, it may even be partially eaten.  While not a ‘primitive’ organism, the antlerworms belong to a group that split off from the main quadrilaterian branch hundreds of millions of years ago. While the branch containing the birrin maintained its stalked eyes and sensory tentacles in many cases, they presently play no role in feeding. However, as revealed by fossils such as the BASKETWORM, what become eyestalks in the birrin were originally lophophoroid structures evolved to catch food via filter feeding. Rather than reducing their role in prey capture, the branch that become antlerworms vastly increased the size and strength of these organs, using them as powerful tentacles capable of both sensing and grasping prey. The eye spots, initially at the ends of the tentacles, evolved downwards and away from the vulnerable tips to nearer the body and are thus protected from struggling food. These adaptations offer scientists a window into the early role of quadrilatarian sensory tentacles, and why, even if not directly involved in feeding among the birrin and their relatives, remain evolutionarily important to the group today.”

title: Religion in Plato and Cicero
description: Rexine, John E. Religion in Plato and Cicero . Philosophical Library [New York], 1959. Chapter I – General Introduction Historical, Political, and Philosophical Context: Rexine introduces the work by situating Plato and Cicero as seminal figures in their respective cultures—Plato as a foundational philosopher of the Greek polis, and Cicero as Rome’s philosophical statesman. He explains that both authors use the Laws as vehicles for moral and civic instruction, emphasizing religion's place in political life. The chapter justifies isolating religion for comparative study, even if such separation would be alien to ancient thinkers. Epistemology: Religion is approached as something revealed through text and custom, but also analyzed via rational discourse. Rexine foreshadows Plato’s deductive reasoning and Cicero’s cultural intuition as key epistemological methods. Ontology: The chapter hints at contrasting ontological frameworks: Plato sees a cosmos ruled by rational soul-like forces, while Cicero operates within a civic reality infused with divine tradition. Ethical/Moral Framework: Both thinkers regard religion as ethically necessary—Plato for justice and order, Cicero for duty and social cohesion. Logical Structure: Rexine explains that his structure will be textual and comparative, proceeding through Plato’s Laws , especially Book X, and then Cicero’s De Legibus Book II. Rhetorical Devices: Plato’s dialectic versus Cicero’s Roman dialogue (with Atticus and Quintus) is presented as a stylistic contrast—philosophical rigor vs. moral persuasion. Implicit Assumptions: The assumption is that classical religion cannot be disentangled from civic identity. Also, that religion is functional: it serves to unify, stabilize, and legitimize law. Applications to Modern Life: The introduction raises the enduring question: should religion be the basis of civic life? It previews issues like religious pluralism, secular law, and natural rights. Student Prompts: Why is it useful—or problematic—to isolate religion as a separate category in classical philosophy? How might Plato’s and Cicero’s attitudes inform debates over religion in modern law and education? Chapter II – Religion in Plato’s Laws Context: This chapter surveys religious content across the twelve books of Plato’s Laws . Rexine frames the Laws as a “second-best” constitution, more practical than the Republic . Religion appears throughout, but receives theological concentration in Book X. Epistemology: Plato’s knowledge of the divine arises from rational metaphysics. Religious practice must align with cosmic truth, not merely tradition. Knowledge of the gods is tied to reason and virtue. Ontology: The divine is a rational soul-force that structures the cosmos. The universe is governed by Nous (intellect), and the ideal state must reflect this cosmic order. Ethics: Piety is obedience to cosmic justice. A just soul mirrors the harmony of the universe. Impious acts disrupt both personal and civic order. Logic: Plato uses a deductive system: from universal motion and order, he argues for the necessity of divine causation (Book X). His political theology follows from first principles. Rhetoric: Myths, analogies (e.g., God as the straight line), and moral exhortation are used. He frames the lawgiver as both rational and divinely inspired. Assumptions: Religious law must be state-regulated. Private worship threatens civic unity. The gods are moral exemplars and cannot be bribed—contrary to popular belief. Modern Application: Raises enduring questions about the regulation of religion: Should states suppress “heresy”? Can religion be a basis for law in pluralistic societies? Prompts: Should religion be state-controlled, as Plato suggests? Why or why not? How does Plato justify the punishment of religious dissenters? Chapter III – The Theology of Book X of Plato’s Laws Context: This chapter is a deep dive into Plato’s only systematic theology. Rexine calls it the first rational demonstration of God's existence in Western literature. It is meant to refute atheism, Epicurean-style indifference, and sacrificial bribery. Epistemology: Knowledge of the divine comes from reason and observation of cosmic order. Plato argues from causation, motion, and order—his is a proto-natural theology. Ontology: God is a soul—specifically, a self-moving principle. This soul is good, intelligent, and governs the universe. All motion stems from this divine soul. Ethics: The moral order is inseparable from divine order. Souls are rewarded or punished according to cosmic justice. Even in death, the soul receives what it deserves. Logic: The argument follows a deductive chain: motion → self-motion → soul → divine soul → cosmic law → divine justice. Rhetoric: Plato uses analogies (e.g., wolves bribing watchdogs) to ridicule common superstitions. He crafts a moral cosmology. Assumptions: God is good and just; irreligion is a threat to civic harmony. The state must educate and discipline belief. Application: This raises issues for religious liberty: can belief be coerced? Should theology be taught as civic duty? Prompts: Compare Plato’s argument from motion to modern arguments for God’s existence. How does Plato link cosmology to moral behavior? Chapter IV – Religion in Cicero’s Laws Context: This chapter turns to Roman thought. Rexine shows that Cicero’s De Legibus is modeled on Plato’s Laws but rooted in Roman tradition. Religion is contained mainly in Book II. Epistemology: Cicero’s knowledge of the divine comes from cultural memory, practice, and Stoic natural law. He emphasizes universal belief, ancestral tradition, and reason. Ontology: The gods exist and are rational; man has a “divine spark” or “kinship” (agnatio) with them. The soul is immortal and virtuous souls are near-divine. Ethics: Civic virtue is rooted in religion. Piety, moderation, and ancestral custom are central to Roman identity. Religion upholds law and prevents moral collapse. Logic: Cicero relies more on rhetorical appeal than syllogistic argument. His logic is cultural and intuitive rather than metaphysical. Rhetoric: He invokes Rome’s mos maiorum, oaths, ancestral temples, and national festivals. His religious language affirms rather than questions. Assumptions: Roman religious tradition is valid and sufficient. Civic unity depends on reverence for gods and rituals. Private cults are suspect. Application: Raises questions about nationalism and religion—how much should tradition guide policy? What if the tradition is unjust? Prompts: How does Cicero’s religious thought reflect Roman patriotism? Compare Cicero’s divine-human kinship with Plato’s theology of separation. Chapter V – Cicero and Roman Religious Practice Historical, Political, and Philosophical Context: This chapter examines how Cicero’s theoretical work in De Legibus aligns with (or departs from) Roman religious custom. Rexine highlights that Cicero, while philosophical, is ultimately a civic traditionalist. He embeds religious law within Roman institutions: priesthoods, augury, ancestral festivals, and household cults. Unlike Plato’s rational theocracy, Cicero’s religiosity is culturally inherited and stabilizing. Style of Epistemology: Religious knowledge is transmitted through mos maiorum (ancestral custom), priestly interpretation, and state ceremony—not personal revelation or philosophical demonstration. This collective wisdom is assumed valid and effective. Ontology: The gods are real, moral, and interested in Roman society. Divinity is not abstract but embodied in rituals, offices (e.g., pontifex maximus), and the visible city. The cosmos and city mirror each other—order above sustains order below. Ethical or Moral Framework: Pietas (piety) is the foremost civic virtue. Religious observance sustains the res publica . Impiety (e.g., neglect of rituals or innovation in worship) threatens both divine favor and social cohesion. Proper rites maintain justice, peace, and Roman identity. Logical Structure and Reasoning Style: Rather than formal logic, Cicero uses analogical reasoning: because Rome endured through its religious institutions, they must be preserved. He argues from continuity, precedent, and moral sentiment. Rhetorical Devices and Forms: Cicero draws from legal diction, oratory, and patriotic memory. He cites Roman laws and historic figures (e.g., Numa, Scipio) as exemplars. His tone is prescriptive, meant to educate statesmen. Hidden or Implicit Assumptions: Civic peace depends on religious orthodoxy. Roman religion is best because it works. There is no distinction between civil law and sacred law—Rome’s laws are quasi-divine. Applications to Modern Ethical or Civic Life: The chapter invites questions about tradition-based governance. Should laws evolve beyond ancestral precedent? What if religious tradition suppresses minority views or rights? Discussion Questions and Essay Prompts: In what ways does Cicero tie religion to national identity and law? Is religion in Cicero more about belief or about public ritual? Can civic stability be maintained without religious unity? Chapter VI – Plato and Cicero: General Conclusions Context: This comparative chapter synthesizes the main similarities and differences in how Plato and Cicero view religion’s role in law and civic life. Rexine aims to show how deeply embedded religious belief is in both their legal-political projects—even though one is metaphysically rigorous and the other historically conservative. Epistemology: Plato prioritizes reason and metaphysical argument to arrive at theological truth. Cicero relies on inherited wisdom and Stoic natural law. Both see knowledge of the divine as essential for public virtue, but they disagree on how it is acquired and transmitted. Ontology: Plato’s divine is abstract and soul-based—God is pure reason in motion. Cicero’s divine is more anthropomorphic and grounded in civic reality. However, both assume a moral cosmos governed by intelligible law. Ethical Framework: Both thinkers connect personal morality with civic religion. Impiety is not just a private vice but a public threat. The good citizen is also the pious one, and law depends on religious conscience. Logic and Structure: Plato builds a deductive theology of divine justice; Cicero uses analogy, historical precedent, and rhetorical appeals. Cicero avoids Plato’s metaphysical burdens, focusing instead on what works for Rome. Rhetoric: Plato uses the dialogue to lead the soul toward higher truth. Cicero uses dialogue as civic instruction and cultural reinforcement. Both aim to persuade, but their audiences and methods differ. Hidden Assumptions: Plato assumes that truth can be rationally known and imposed via law. Cicero assumes that the Roman system is morally exemplary and should be preserved. Both assert a link between theology and legitimacy. Applications: Modern political philosophy must grapple with these two models: the philosophical-theocratic republic of Plato and the traditionalist, quasi-constitutional Rome of Cicero. Both offer lessons—and warnings—for debates on law, religion, and public morality. Prompts: How does each thinker justify religion’s central role in civic law? Which model—Platonic or Ciceronian—best suits a modern republic? Can law be both secular and morally grounded? Chapter VII – The Platonic Attitude Toward Poetry Context: This final chapter is a coda to the religious discussion. Rexine explores Plato’s infamous censorship of poetry in Laws and Republic , and how religious orthodoxy shapes his aesthetics. Plato fears that poetry misleads citizens about the gods, virtue, and reality. He treats poets as dangerous unless they serve moral and civic truth. Epistemology: Poetry is not a path to truth—it is mimesis (imitation), and often deceptive. True knowledge comes from philosophy, which has access to reality through reason. Ontology: Poets present gods as flawed and immoral, contradicting Plato’s ordered, rational cosmos. Therefore, their representations are ontologically corrupt—they misstate what is. Ethics: Since poetry affects the soul, especially the young, it must align with civic virtue. Only hymns and morally edifying works are permitted. Artistic freedom is subordinated to the good of the city. Logic: Plato draws from the idea that education shapes the soul. Bad representations lead to bad habits; therefore, misleading poetry leads to moral degeneration. Rhetoric: Plato uses strong imagery—comparing poets to corruptors or irresponsible nurses. He offers a regulatory framework: censor poems, approve hymns, ban “dangerous” myths. Assumptions: Art is powerful but dangerous. The good city cannot tolerate aesthetic freedom that contradicts moral truth. This aligns with his theological insistence on correct belief. Applications: Raises questions about censorship, artistic liberty, and education. Should governments regulate moral content in media and the arts? Who defines what is “virtuous” or “true”? Prompts: Why does Plato fear poetry? Is his concern valid in modern media? Should art be free from religious or civic constraints? Compare Plato’s view of the poet with Cicero’s use of cultural memory. Who better integrates art and public virtue? Side-by-Side Comparison Chart: Plato vs. Cicero on Religion and Law Based on John E. Rexine’s Religion in Plato and Cicero (1959) Category Plato ( Laws ) Cicero ( De Legibus ) Historical Role of Religion Essential to the philosophical constitution of the state. Religion forms the spine of civic order and morality. Integral to the Roman Republic as inherited tradition; religion upholds civic identity and continuity. Source of Religious Knowledge (Epistemology) Rational inquiry and observation of cosmic order (e.g., Book X’s proof from motion). Cultural memory, ancestral tradition ( mos maiorum ), and Stoic-influenced natural law. Concept of the Divine (Ontology) God is a self-moving, rational soul; the cosmos is governed by nous . Multiple souls may exist, but divine reason dominates. Gods are personal, moral, and relational. Humanity shares a kinship ( agnatio ) with the divine through the rational soul. Ethical Function of Religion Piety is necessary for virtue; the good man mirrors divine order. Impiety disrupts both soul and state. Pietas (dutiful respect) is a civic virtue. Religious observance sustains justice, law, and social trust. Religious Law & Enforcement Strict public regulation of worship. Private cults and impiety punished—often by death. Heresy is a crime. Public religion is regulated through priesthoods and festivals. Private worship discouraged, but enforcement is less philosophical, more civic. View of Priests and Religious Officials Priests are carefully selected moral exemplars, guardians of cosmic and civic order. Priests (e.g., pontifices , augures ) uphold Roman tradition and law. Some offices are hereditary. Attitude Toward Theology Constructs the first “natural theology.” Proves existence of divine soul and cosmic justice through reason. Accepts the existence of gods as cultural and natural law. Theology is less formal but framed within Stoicism. Purpose of Ritual and Worship To align human behavior with cosmic order. Only the virtuous can offer acceptable sacrifices. To maintain civic harmony, uphold tradition, and foster gratitude. Ritual is practical and ancestral. Attitude Toward Poets & Art Poets are distrusted; their works must be censored unless aligned with virtue and truth. Poets and orators preserve mos maiorum and inspire Roman ideals. Less censorious than Plato. Ultimate Religious Goal A harmonious city where citizens reflect the divine order through just laws and philosophical understanding. A stable republic rooted in ancestral religion, moral tradition, and shared civic identity. Glossary of Key Classical Terms Term Definition and Relevance Pietas Roman virtue of religious and civic duty, including reverence for the gods, ancestors, and homeland. Central in Cicero. Nous Greek for “mind” or “intellect.” In Plato, it refers to the divine ordering principle of the universe. Daemon (δαίμων) In Greek thought, a spiritual intermediary between gods and humans. For Plato, often linked to divine aspects of the soul. Nomos (νόμος) Greek for “law,” encompassing both divine/cosmic law and human legislation. Central to Plato’s concept of just society. Mos Maiorum Latin for “the custom of the ancestors.” A foundational concept in Roman law, religion, and morality. Vital for Cicero. Psychē (ψυχή) The soul or animating principle in Greek philosophy. Plato identifies it as the source of motion and moral judgment. Lex / Leges Latin for “law/laws.” Cicero’s De Legibus emphasizes the divinely sanctioned nature of Roman law. Eusebeia (ε ὐ σέβεια) Greek concept of piety or reverence, especially toward the gods. Analogous to Roman pietas . Agnatio Latin for kinship or lineage. Cicero uses it to suggest humans are spiritual kin of the gods through reason. Sacra Privata Private (family-based) religious rites in Rome. Regulated by the state; discouraged if they threatened public order. Pontifex Maximus Chief priest of Rome, overseeing public religion. For Cicero, a civic and sacred office. Heresy Not a classical term per se, but Plato's legal theology anticipates later concepts of heresy as deviance from sacred law.

title: Trading View Indicator Settings Explained
description: TradingView Indicator Settings Explained Ever opened up a stock or crypto chart and felt completely overwhelmed by all the squiggly lines? It happens to the best of us. When you're just starting out, charting platforms can look like an alien dashboard. It’s easy to feel like you need a math degree just to figure out what’s going on. But honestly, it gets a lot easier once you know how to tweak things to fit your personal style. If you’ve been looking to have TradingView indicator settings explained in plain English, you’re in the right place. Let’s break down exactly how you can customize your charts without the headache. TradingView Indicator Settings Explained: What Are They Exactly? Before we start clicking buttons, let's talk about what these tools actually do. Think of indicators as special visual filters for your charts. They take raw, boring price data and turn it into visual clues. This helps you figure out the trend and guess where a stock or crypto might go next. But here’s the thing: the default settings you see aren’t a one-size-fits-all magic pill. It’s kind of like buying a new car. The very first thing you do is adjust the seat, tweak the mirrors, and set up your favorite radio stations so it fits you . Indicator settings do exactly that for your trading. They let you change the length of time, the visual colors, and the sensitivity of the tools you're using. For example, a day trader might want a super sensitive Moving Average to catch quick moves. On the flip side, a long-term investor will dial it back to look at the bigger, multi-month picture. How to Customize Chart Tools: A Step-by-Step Guide Ready to clean up your workspace? It’s actually pretty fun once you get the hang of it. Here’s exactly how to add and adjust your tools, step by step. 1. Add your chosen indicator to the chart First things first, click the "Indicators" button right at the top of your screen. Type in whatever you want to use—like the RSI (Relative Strength Index) or a basic Moving Average—and click it to add it to your chart. 2. Find the little gear icon Now, look at the top-left corner of your actual chart. You'll see the name of the indicator you just added. Hover your mouse over that name, and a small menu will pop up. Click the gear icon to open up your settings menu. 3. Tweak the 'Inputs' tab This is the math part, but don't panic. The "Inputs" tab lets you change the timeframe or length of the data. If you change a Moving Average length from 9 to 50, it stops looking at the last 9 candles and calculates the last 50 instead. Tip: If you're a total beginner, it's totally okay to leave the math alone until you're more comfortable. 4. Customize the 'Style' tab This is the fun, creative part. Under the "Style" tab, you can change line colors, make lines thicker, or turn off messy background shading. The goal here is to make your charts easy on your eyes so you can read them fast. 5. Save your new setup as a default Did you find a color combo and input setup you absolutely love? Don't lose it! Click the "Defaults" button at the bottom of the settings box and hit "Save as default." Now you don't have to redo all this work every single time you open a chart. 5 Common Mistakes When Tweaking Technical Indicators It's super easy to get carried away when you first discover all these customization options. Try to avoid these classic rookie traps so you don't overcomplicate your trading. Mistake 1: Turning your chart into a rainbow spaghetti bowl Adding 15 different indicators won't make you a better trader. It’ll honestly just confuse you and hide the actual price candles. Keep it clean. Stick to 2 or 3 tools that actually make sense to your brain. Mistake 2: Messing with the inputs too soon The default math (like a 14-day RSI) is the default for a really good reason—it works well for most people. Don't go changing these numbers randomly unless you have a specific, backtested strategy in mind. Mistake 3: Ignoring the "Visibility" tab You probably don't need a massive weekly trend line showing up on your tiny 5-minute day trading chart. Use the visibility settings to hide certain indicators on timeframes where they just don't belong. Mistake 4: Using terrible color combinations Red and green are standard, but if you use TradingView in dark mode, dark blue or dark purple lines are going to be invisible. Make your lines pop with bright, contrasting colors so you can read them at a quick glance. Mistake 5: Blindly copying the internet gurus Just because a popular YouTuber uses a 200-day moving average in neon pink doesn't mean you have to do the exact same thing. Tweak things to fit your eyes, your screen size, and your personal trading style. FAQs About TradingView Indicator Settings Explained Still have a few questions? Here are a few things beginners usually ask when setting up their charts. Do I need a paid TradingView account to change settings? Nope! Free users can absolutely adjust the style, colors, and inputs of their indicators. The only catch is that free accounts are limited to a maximum of 3 indicators per chart at one time. How do I reset an indicator back to normal? Messed something up and your chart looks crazy? No worries, it happens. Just open the indicator settings via the gear icon, look for the "Defaults" button at the bottom right, and click "Reset settings." You’re right back to square one. What are the best indicator settings for day trading? There isn't a single perfect answer, but day traders usually prefer faster, more sensitive settings. For example, using a 9-period Moving Average helps you see short-term, rapid price action a lot clearer than a slow 200-period one. Conclusion Getting the hang of your chart tools doesn't have to be a stressful, frustrating experience. Once you dive in and start clicking around, you'll quickly realize that the platform is actually pretty intuitive. Having TradingView indicator settings explained gives you a great head start, but the real learning happens when you get your hands dirty. Don't be afraid to experiment with different colors, thicknesses, and inputs to see what makes the most sense to you. So, open up a blank chart, throw on a new indicator, and start playing around with the settings. Which tool are you going to test out first? Go ahead and give it a try right now! title: THE EVIL
author: Sorin Cerin
description: SORIN CERIN - BIBLIOGRAPHY Sorin Cerin  ( Born :  November 25, 1963,  Baia Mare   , Romania ) is an important existentialist poet from the 21st century, quoted next to Sartre or Kierkegaard, philosopher,- the creator of Coaxialism, – compared to Schopenhauer, Nietzsche and Wittgenstein. Sorin Cerin is particularly sought after by the great public for the 11,486 structured aphorisms in 14 volumes of thoughts previously published in various publishing houses, and then to be reunited under the aegis of a monumental volume called  Wisdom Collection , a title that brought him celebrity and international recognition, for which he is considered to be one of the most representative thinkers of the aphoristic genre in the world, and the thoughts of this work are selected in various prestigious publications or world anthologies. Also, the essays and novels should not be ignored because it recommends him as an essayist and novelist as deep as his poetic, philosophical or aphoristic works. ( Wisdom Collection – Complete Works of Aphorisms – Reference Edition  ) FAMOUS QUOTES BY SORIN CERIN: Only in the eyes of love you can find infinity.” ― Sorin Cerin,  Wisdom Collection: The Book of except the heart.” ― Sorin Cerin,  Wisdom Collection: The Book of Wisdom “ The dawn of beauty always comes after night.” ― Sorin Cerin,  Wisdom Collection: The Book of Wisdom “Where I will find peace
